# Prop 37 endorsement: Buying a home in California can feel impossible. Is this the fix?

## Most down-payment assistance programs for home buyers drive up housing costs. Prop 37 is different.

S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements

By [Chronicle Editorial Board](https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/), Opinion StaffSep 15, 2026

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sfchronicle.com%2Fopinion%2Feditorials%2Farticle%2Fprop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php%3Futm_campaign%3DCMS%2520Sharing%2520Tools%2520\(Premium\)%26utm_source%3Dfacebook.com%26utm_medium%3Dreferral)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sfchronicle.com%2Fopinion%2Feditorials%2Farticle%2Fprop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php%3Futm_campaign%3DCMS%2520Sharing%2520Tools%2520\(Premium\)%26utm_source%3Dt.co%26utm_medium%3Dreferral&text=Prop%2037%20endorsement%3A%20Buying%20a%20home%20in%20California%20can%20feel%20impossible.%20Is%20this%20the%20fix%3F&via=sfchronicle)[](https://bsky.app/intent/compose?text=Prop%2037%20endorsement%3A%20Buying%20a%20home%20in%20California%20can%20feel%20impossible.%20Is%20this%20the%20fix%3F%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sfchronicle.com%2Fopinion%2Feditorials%2Farticle%2Fprop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sfchronicle.com%2Fopinion%2Feditorials%2Farticle%2Fprop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php%3Futm_campaign%3DCMS%2520Sharing%2520Tools%2520\(Premium\)%26utm_source%3Dbsky.app%26utm_medium%3Dreferral)[](mailto:?subject=Your%20friend%20has%20shared%20a%20San%20Francisco%20Chronicle%20link%20with%20you%3A&body=Prop%2037%20endorsement%3A%20Buying%20a%20home%20in%20California%20can%20feel%20impossible.%20Is%20this%20the%20fix%3F%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.sfchronicle.com%2Fopinion%2Feditorials%2Farticle%2Fprop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php%3Futm_campaign%3DCMS%2520Sharing%2520Tools%2520\(Premium\)%26utm_source%3Dshare-by-email%26utm_medium%3Demail%0A%0AOPINION%3A%20Most%20down-payment%20assistance%20programs%20for%20home%20buyers%20drive%20up%20housing%20costs.%20Prop%2037%20is%20different%2C%20the%20Chronicle%20editorial%20board%20writes.%0A%0AThis%20message%20was%20sent%20via%20San%20Francisco%20Chronicle)

It’s no secret that buying a home in California is a grim and mostly futile undertaking.

In the Bay Area, you need to make about $444,000 a year just to purchase a mid-priced home, [according to a May report from the real estate brokerage Redfin](https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/home-buy-income-bay-area-22281201.php). A [2025 Zillow study found](https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/mortgage-rate-bay-area-20792146.php) that even if mortgage rates fell to 0%, most Bay Area families still couldn’t comfortably afford to buy.

Statewide, the median home price hovers around $900,000, [according to the California Association of Realtors](https://carorg.sharepoint.com/:x:/s/CAR-RE-PublicProducts/IQAK-pU7cef4QpkWsCPlxwZKAbdKLa3OO0vFwHpuH_FADK8?rtime=9NSXc_YN30g). That puts a traditional 20% down payment out of reach for many families, locking them out of a pathway to generational wealth while simultaneously reducing the state’s political muscle as [residents flee](https://www.ppic.org/blog/whos-leaving-california-and-whos-moving-in/) to cheaper, [primarily red](https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/housing-development-california-state-21027403.php), states. 

[Proposition 37](https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot promises to help solve these problems by making it easier for middle-class Californians to enter homeownership. 

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The measure would permit the state to loan middle-income residents up to 17% of the cost of newly constructed houses, townhomes, row houses, condominiums and manufactured homes. Families with a traditional mortgage would only have to put 3% down.  

Under Prop 37 in San Francisco, a family would need $40,000 for a median-priced home of about $1.3 million — compared to a 20% down payment of about $267,000.  

Californians are clamoring for down payment help. When the state launched a down payment assistance program for first-time homebuyers in 2023, the [$300 million on offer was spoken for in less than two weeks](https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/california-home-buyer-assistance-program-17888975.php).

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

But Prop 37 takes a different tack than traditional efforts like that one.

To start, [it wouldn’t cost taxpayers a dime](https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop37-110326.pdf).  

The measure would authorize the California Housing Finance Agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds — which would be repaid by homeowners’ monthly loan and interest payments, not by taxpayers. Loan payments would also cover the administrative costs of the program, which will undergo an annual independent audit. 

Nor will the measure drive up housing prices by subsidizing demand.

Only new homes explicitly constructed under the rules of the measure are eligible for Prop 37 loans. This incentivizes development instead of simply allowing more buyers to compete for a limited supply of existing homes.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Prop 37 aims to juice construction by eliminating red tape, particularly for condos. 

Although condos are often the most affordable option for would-be homeowners, their production has fallen dramatically in California due to the state’s “right to repair” law, [which effectively encourages homeowners to sue developers](https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/condo-home-california-law-22306098.php) for alleged construction defects — even easily fixable ones that aren’t harmful. 

This year, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, attempted a fix with [a bill](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB1903) that would have comprehensively overhauled California’s right-to-repair law. 

But it [died in the final moments of the legislative session](https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/09/condo-construction-bill-dies/?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=WhatMatters&utm_source=31&npnl=NTA2MTM0fDc4YTAyODgwNzMxZGY1NThiZTI5MGVlZGUxOTA2Y2VhYzNlNTFlMGM3YTJkYTNhNjZiNzFhZTljYzM1Njg5ODM&utm_source=ActiveCampaign&utm_medium=email&utm_content=Is%20Gavin%20Newsom%20in%20his%20lame%20duck%20era%3F&utm_campaign=WhatMatters) — even after being significantly watered down. 

Prop 37 would reanimate some aspects of Wicks’ bill. 

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

It would require claimants to clearly specify each alleged violation and permit them to release builders from liability if repairs are completed satisfactorily. It also incentivizes quick resolution of lawsuits — builders could ask courts to dismiss actions against them if claimants drag their feet — and caps attorneys’ fees at 30% of total recovery.  

With legislative reform in limbo, “the condo defect implications of Prop 37 are solid,” Leora Tanjuatco Ross, YIMBY Action’s California director, told the editorial board. 

We certainly hope that lawmakers pursue more transformative defect reform in the future. But until that happens, Prop 37 could serve as a stopgap. 

The ability of middle-class buyers to finance a home, such as these along Kirkwood Avenue in San Francisco, seen on April 9, 2022, would be enhanced with the passage of S.F.’s Prop 37 in November. Justin Katigbak/For the S.F. Chronicle

The measure also requires builders who want to take advantage of these right-to-repair reforms to meet certain labor standards, such as providing workers’ compensation and unemployment insurance, while abiding by state and local laws requiring prevailing wage — or union-level pay — for large-scale projects. 

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Those who have lived in California for at least a year and have a family income of 80% to 200% of the area median income — which in San Francisco [ranges from about $104,000 to $260,000 for a family of two](https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/2026_AMI-IncomeLimits-HMFA.pdf) — are eligible for Prop 37 loans.

No, you can’t use Prop 37 for a second home; qualifying homes must be the buyer’s primary residence. Eligible home prices are capped, too — they can’t be sold for more than 125% of the conforming loan limit for a one-unit property in the county in question, which is about $1.5 million in San Francisco. 

The measure also contains consumer protections. For instance, it requires the program’s mortgage loans to be fixed-rate and instructs the California Housing Finance Agency to set them “as low as possible.” It also permits the agency to establish a homeowner education requirement. 

Just how affordable these loans would be, however, is an open question. [As a California Budget Center analysis noted](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/will-proposition-37-make-homeownership-more-affordable-its-not-guaranteed/#h-how-is-prop-37-different-from-california-s-existing-downpayment-assistance-programs), the Housing Finance Agency’s loans may come with higher-than-usual interest rates because they’re second mortgages. Investors view these as riskier than first mortgages, which are repaid first if a homeowner defaults. 

Former state Sen. Bob Hertzberg, a Democrat from Los Angeles County who collected signatures to put Prop 37 on the ballot, told the editorial board that he believes the measure could create 190,000 homes and spur $150 billion in economic activity. 

That certainly sounds transformative. But is the measure likely to live up to Hertzberg’s hype?

Prop 37 has no formal opposition and most experts we spoke with were cautiously supportive.

The measure technically didn’t need to go to the ballot; the Legislature or housing finance agency could have established the program. We’re not a fan of politicians using the ballot for their vanity projects, and there’s certainly some ego at play for Hertzberg, who referred to the homes that could be built under Prop 37 as “Hertzberg houses.”  

But Hertzberg [did try to get the Legislature to approve a version of the program](https://shou.senate.ca.gov/sites/shou.senate.ca.gov/files/7.%20SB%201457%20%28Hertzberg%29%20-%20analysis.pdf), to no avail. 

“I’m just a burnt-out old politician trying to do the right thing who hasn’t lost his soul, and I might help the motherf—ers in the middle class if I die doing it,” said Hertzberg, who clearly [subscribes to the John Burton school of profanity.](https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/john-burton-obituary-17820175.php) 

About Opinion

The editorial positions of The Chronicle, including election recommendations, represent the **consensus of the editorial board**, consisting of the publisher, the editorial page editor and staff members of the opinion pages. Its judgments are made **independent of the news operation**, which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.

Prop 37’s scope is limited enough that we don’t think it will fundamentally change California’s housing landscape. But given how dire our housing crisis is, any positive impact is better than none at all. 

We recommend a yes vote.

It’s Not Guaranteed.”** It examines Proposition 37 (on the November 2026 California ballot), which would create a “middle-class homeownership loan” program. The measure would authorize the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to provide down-payment assistance of up to 17% of the purchase price for qualifying newly built homes (or newly converted units), with buyers contributing at least 3% of their own funds. Combined, this would reach a 20% down payment, eliminating private mortgage insurance, while a conventional first mortgage covers the rest. Eligibility includes California residency, household income up to 200% of area median income (AMI, which varies widely by county), and home price caps of roughly $1 million to $1.5 million depending on location. Recipients would not need to be first-time buyers, and the state would not take a share of home appreciation.[[1]](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/will-proposition-37-make-homeownership-more-affordable-its-not-guaranteed/)

The analysis concludes that it is unclear whether the program would meaningfully improve homeownership affordability for “middle-class” Californians facing the greatest barriers, and it highlights several potential drawbacks.

### Second Mortgage Structure and Monthly Costs
A core distinction from existing CalHFA programs (such as MyHome Assistance or Dream for All) is that Prop. 37 assistance would be provided as a **loan, not a grant**, and recipients are **likely to repay it monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage**. This would be in addition to payments on the conventional first mortgage. Existing programs typically use deferred “silent second” mortgages (with little or no interest accruing until sale, refinance, or payoff of the first mortgage), so they do not compete with monthly household expenses like groceries or utilities.[[1]](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/will-proposition-37-make-homeownership-more-affordable-its-not-guaranteed/)

Prop. 37’s structure stems from the revenue bonds, which by law must be repaid from the program’s own proceeds (principal and interest on the second mortgages issued). The measure also includes language allowing borrowers to request a temporary hardship deferral of monthly interest payments, which the Budget Center interprets as confirming the intended monthly-payment design. The second mortgage’s interest rate would be set later by CalHFA based on bond terms and market conditions (with an intent to keep costs as low as possible, but no guarantee of below-market rates). Because second-lien mortgages are riskier for investors (the first mortgage is repaid first in a default), investors may demand a higher return. This could result in second-mortgage rates **above** conventional first-mortgage rates (around 6.5% at the time of the analysis). The actual rate would not be known until after voters decide. Overall, while the program could help buyers reach 20% down, the added monthly second-mortgage payments “could erode much of the benefit.”[[1]](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/will-proposition-37-make-homeownership-more-affordable-its-not-guaranteed/)

### Other Affordability and Equity Concerns
Even a 3% down payment could be a significant barrier. For example, it would be $15,000 on a $500,000 home or $21,000 on a $700,000 home. The median amount in Californians’ checking and savings accounts was just over $18,000 (in 2025 dollars), so this could deplete most or all of a typical family’s liquid savings. The high AMI cap (e.g., up to $166,800 for a family of four in Madera County or $375,800 in Santa Clara County) and lack of a first-time or first-generation buyer requirement mean the program may disproportionately benefit higher-income eligible households rather than those with the greatest barriers. Racial and ethnic disparities in income, wealth, credit, and existing homeownership rates could mean White families (already overrepresented among homeowners) benefit more, while Black and Latinx families (underrepresented in the “middle-class” income range and more likely to be renters) face greater challenges.[[1]](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/will-proposition-37-make-homeownership-more-affordable-its-not-guaranteed/)

Restricting aid to new construction could also encourage sprawl (pushing development to suburban/exurban areas farther from jobs, with environmental and equity impacts) and add other costs common to new homes, such as HOA dues (more prevalent in new construction, averaging around $280/month nationally with potential annual increases), Mello-Roos assessments, and insurance challenges in wildfire-prone areas. These factors could further undercut purported affordability gains, with benefits skewing toward families already better positioned financially.[[1]](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/will-proposition-37-make-homeownership-more-affordable-its-not-guaranteed/)

The Budget Center takes no position on the measure (it is a nonpartisan research organization) and notes that a similar program could have been created legislatively or by CalHFA without a ballot initiative, as revenue bonds do not require voter approval. Supporters include former Senate Majority Leader Bob Hertzberg (the primary sponsor), some unions, and real estate groups; there were no official opponents listed as of mid-2026 in the analysis. Other sources, such as CalMatters and the Legislative Analyst’s Office, provide additional context on implementation details and potential limited uptake due to monthly costs.[[2]](https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/)

# Will Prop. 37 Make Homeownership More Affordable? It’s Not Guaranteed

Understanding How Proposition 37 Could Affect Homeownership Affordability

August 2026 | By [Monica Davalos](https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/), [Nishi Nair](https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/nishi-nair/), and [Kristin Schumacher](https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kristin-schumacher/)

Print Report 

![Single family homes under construction on an empty street](https://calbudgetcenter.org/app/uploads/2026/07/iStock-2172287638.webp) 

### key takeaway

Proposition 37 on the November 2026 ballot would establish a “middle-class” homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. This assistance could only be used to purchase newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser. The program is intended to be self-sustaining because participating homebuyers — not the state — would ultimately repay the bonds through their mortgage payments.

### table of contents

*   [What Would Prop. 37 Do?](#h-what-would-prop-37-do)
*   [How Would Income Eligibility for Prop. 37’s Downpayment Assistance Vary Across California Counties?](#h-how-would-income-eligibility-for-prop-37-s-downpayment-assistance-vary-across-california-counties)
*   [How Is Prop. 37 Different from California’s Existing Downpayment Assistance Programs?](#h-how-is-prop-37-different-from-california-s-existing-downpayment-assistance-programs)
*   [Would Prop. 37 Reach “Middle-Class” Californians Facing the Greatest Barriers to Homeownership?](#h-would-prop-37-reach-middle-class-californians-facing-the-greatest-barriers-to-homeownership)
*   [Could Prop. 37 Encourage Sprawl and Harm the Environment?](#h-could-prop-37-encourage-sprawl-and-harm-the-environment)
*   [What Other Homeownership Costs Could Come with Prop. 37’s New-Construction Requirement?](#h-what-other-homeownership-costs-could-come-with-prop-37-s-new-construction-requirement)
*   [Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?](#h-who-supports-and-opposes-prop-37)

Supporting homeownership is an important strategy for promoting economic security and wealth building. However, it is unclear whether Prop. 37 would meaningfully help “middle class” Californians who face the greatest barriers to homeownership to afford a home.

As Prop. 37 would be financed through revenue bonds — which do not require voter approval — the program proposed by this initiative could have been enacted legislatively or a comparable program could have been established by the California Finance Housing Agency. Prop. 37 is a citizens’ initiative spearheaded by former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg.

## **What Would Prop. 37 Do?**

The [Middle Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) would direct the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to establish a middle-class homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. The new program would:

*   **Provide up to 17% of the purchase price toward the down payment**, which could only be used to purchase new homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser.
*   **Require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price toward the down payment.** Combined with the 17% state downpayment assistance, this would reach 20% of the home’s purchase price and eliminates the need for private mortgage insurance. A conventional first mortgage would cover the remaining amount.
*   **Require the downpayment assistance to be provided as a loan, not a grant, which recipients are likely to pay back monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage**. This would be in addition to the homebuyer’s monthly payments on their conventional first mortgage.
*   ****Allow applicants to have** incomes up to 200% of the Area Median Income (AMI)**, which varies by region.
*   **Cap the maximum home purchase price at roughly $1 million to $1.5 million,** depending on the county and other factors. This is equivalent to a  $170,000-$255,000 downpayment assistance cap per home.
*   **Not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers**, **nor would recipients owe the state any equity gained in their home.** These are requirements of comparable state downpayment assistance programs the state currently operates.
*   **Allow home builders to become “qualified builders,”** and have their developments automatically qualify for the program if they meet specified labor and enforcement standards.

## **How Would Income Eligibility for Prop. 37’s Downpayment Assistance Vary Across California Counties?**

Prop. 37 would make a broad group of Californians eligible for downpayment assistance by allowing family incomes not exceeding 200% of Area Median Income (AMI) to qualify, a threshold that extends well beyond established downpayment assistance programs.

AMI represents the midpoint of family incomes in a specific area, adjusted for household size. In other words, half of households in an area have incomes that exceed 100% AMI and half have incomes below that level, so 200% AMI is roughly *double* what a typical family makes in the area. The limit is tied to local incomes, so whether a family income would qualify for Prop. 37’s downpayment assistance would vary significantly across California.

For example, a Budget Center analysis of Census Bureau data shows that a family of four earning up to $166,800 annually in Madera County or up to $375,800 annually in Santa Clara County could each qualify for assistance. However, the final dollar amounts would be set by CalHFA if Prop. 37 is approved by voters.

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/q17bI/full.png) 

## **How Is Prop. 37 Different from California’s Existing Downpayment Assistance Programs?**

California operates [several](https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/index.htm) statewide homeownership programs through CalHFA, but Prop. 37 would take a different approach that could hit family budgets harder, as participants are likely to pay back the downpayment assistance monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage.

For example, CalHFA’s [MyHome Assistance Program](https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/myhome.htm) and the [Dream for All Shared Appreciation Loan](https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/dream/) program both provide downpayment assistance through deferred “[silent second](https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/myaccount/faqs.htm)” loans (also known as silent second mortgages). MyHome charges 1% simple interest on the assistance; Dream for All accrues no interest, but requires a 15% or 20% share of the home’s appreciation to go to the state. Under both programs, nothing is due on these silent second mortgages until the homeowner sells, refinances, or pays off the first mortgage. This ensures that the downpayment assistance doesn’t compete with the first mortgage, groceries, utility bills, or other basic needs in a family’s monthly budget.

Prop. 37’s approach is likely to require monthly payments. This is because CalHFA would issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, and by law those bonds must be repaid from the proceeds of the program itself — meaning the principal and interest of the second mortgages CalHFA issues. The second mortgages would need to generate steady, ongoing revenue to pay the debt from the revenue bonds. Language in the measure also states “a borrower may request a temporary hardship deferral of monthly interest payments on its middle-class homeownership loan,” further alluding to its intended structure.

Under Prop. 37, the second mortgage payment could also likely carry higher interest rates above conventional first mortgage rates. Although the measure states the intent to provide below-market downpayment assistance financing, it doesn’t guarantee it. The interest rate on the second mortgages would ultimately depend on the terms under which the bonds are issued and market conditions at the time of implementation, which are largely outside CalHFA’s control.

Revenue bonds that finance second mortgages are inherently riskier for investors because if a homeowner defaults, the first mortgage gets repaid before the second, leaving the bond investors more exposed to loss. Investors may therefore require a higher return to compensate for that additional risk, which could increase the interest rate on the second mortgage. This means Prop. 37’s second mortgage rate could land above the roughly 6.5% conventional first-mortgage rates buyers already face today. CalHFA wouldn’t set the actual rate or terms on the second mortgage until implementation, so the interest rate cannot be known before voters decide on Prop. 37.

Ultimately, while Prop. 37 could help get homebuyers to a 20% downpayment to avoid private mortgage insurance, the monthly repayment costs for the second mortgage could erode much of the benefit the downpayment assistance was meant to provide.

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/McRIx/full.png) 

## **Would Prop. 37 Reach “Middle-Class” Californians Facing the Greatest Barriers to Homeownership?**

Prop. 37 would make a broad range of households eligible for downpayment assistance, but income eligibility alone does not determine who can realistically purchase a home. Racial and ethnic disparities in [income](https://www.ppic.org/publication/income-inequality-in-california/#:~:text=Overall%2C%20the%20highest,without%20college%20degrees.), [wealth](https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/#:~:text=Wealth%20gaps%20by%20race%20and%20ethnicity%20are%20large.), [credit access](https://www.epi.org/publication/chasing-the-dream-of-equity/#:~:text=Despite%20the%20bill%E2%80%99s%20intention%20to%20expand%20credit%20access%2C%20Black%20applicants%20are%20consistently%20more%20likely%20to%20be%20denied%20loans%20than%20applicants%20from%20other%20racial%20groups%20\(), and [housing affordability](https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/HAI2025byEthnicity#:~:text=Meanwhile%2C%20only%2011%20percent%20of%20Black%20households%20and%2011%20percent%20of%20Hispanic/Latino%20households%20had%20the%20same%20ability.) mean that not all eligible families across California may be positioned to benefit from the program as proposed.

Prop. 37 would require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price, which would still be unattainable for many Californians. For example:

*   A house that costs $500,000 would require a 3% down payment of $15,000.
*   A house that costs $700,000 would require a 3% down payment of $21,000.

These upfront costs could be out of reach for many families, with the result that Prop. 37’s assistance could largely benefit families with incomes toward the higher end of the eligibility range. According to the Public Policy Institute of California, the median amount in Californians’ checking and savings accounts was [just over $18,000](https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf) in 2025 dollars. This means that a 3% down payment could still almost or entirely clear out most or all of what an average family has in checkings and savings.

Prop. 37 could also reinforce economic, racial, and ethnic inequities in homeownership. The measure is intended to help “middle class” Californians, roughly defined as those with incomes between 80% to 200% AMI. White families are overrepresented among middle- and upper-middle-income Californians (46%), compared to their share of all California families (42%).

In contrast, Black and Latinx families are underrepresented in this “middle class” income range. This means that white families could disproportionately benefit from this program —  even though white households already make up the [largest share of homeowners](https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) in the state, while Black and Latinx renter households face [disproportionately high housing costs](https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CHP_State-Housing-Needs-Report-2025.pdf).

![](https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/8bm0t/full.png) 

Prop. 37 does not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers, further exacerbating equity concerns. Black and brown communities have been [historically excluded from building wealth](https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/) and accumulating assets, making the barrier to entering the housing market even more pronounced. Families of color face [occupational segregation](https://www.americanprogress.org/article/occupational-segregation-in-america/) that pushes them into lower-paying jobs. They are also less likely to [inherit generational wealth](https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/p/2021-12-17-inheritances-by-race/), and are [more likely to be renters.](https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) These factors make it substantially more difficult to save for a down payment, even at similar income levels. Additionally, data limitations often mask [significant disparities in homeownership](https://www.urban.org/urban-wire/why-does-homeownership-vary-so-widely-within-aapi-community) access across racial and ethnic groups, especially among Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander Californians.

## **Could Prop. 37 Encourage Sprawl and Harm the Environment?**

By restricting downpayment assistance to newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, Prop. 37 could push more “middle-class” housing onto land that’s not well suited for housing. Much of the land in California best suited for housing [has already been developed](https://shou.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2025-02/recent-leg-actions-factsheet-updated-feb-2025_0.pdf), leaving remaining areas that are often far from job centers, prone to wildfire,environmentally sensitive, or important for agriculture.

While existing state down payment assistance programs are not immune to these concerns because they can also be used to purchase new homes, Prop. 37 goes further by limiting assistance exclusively to newly constructed homes. As a result, Prop. 37 could further direct “middle-class” housing demand toward suburban and exurban areas. This is a critical deviation from infill development — building on denser, already developed land — which has been the focus of state affordable housing and environmental efforts.

This pattern of building housing on the [periphery of cities](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=IN%20THE%20LAST,a%20city%2C%20is) is known as [urban sprawl](https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf) and carries various environmental and equity considerations. Development in more suburban and inland areas can push Californians further from job centers, increasing their commute times and making it [difficult to travel without a car](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=People%20who%20live%20in%20large%20metropolitan%20areas%20often%20find%20it%20difficult%20to%20travel%20even%20short%20distances%20without%20using%20an%20automobile%2C%20because%20of%20the%20remoteness%20of%20residential%20areas%20and%20inadequate%20availability%20of%20mass%20transit%2C%20walkways%2C%20or%20bike%20paths). It may also encourage development in areas on the outskirts of cities that may cause new homes to [infringe upon natural habitats and important agricultural lands](https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), especially in areas like the Central Valley. Sprawl can also lead to [divestment from urban areas](http://urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), which are often composed of communities of color, and concentrate investment in higher-income, suburban neighborhoods, further exacerbating racial and income inequality across the state.

## **What Other Homeownership Costs Could Come with Prop. 37’s New-Construction Requirement?**

Prop. 37’s new construction requirement could steer homebuyers toward housing with higher out-of-pocket costs on top of their monthly mortgage payments. Unlike existing state down payment assistance programs, which can be used to purchase both new and existing homes, Prop. 37 would limit assistance to newly constructed homes. New construction homes are more likely to come with homeowners association (HOA) dues, Mello-Roos assessments, and home insurance challenges.

HOA fees are far more common in new homes as [nearly 70% of newly built homes](https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-housing-hoa-fees/) listed for sale nationally in 2024 were subject to HOA dues, compared with about 38% of existing homes. In California, more than a third of residents live in an HOA — including about 65% of all California homeowners. The [average monthly fee is $280](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/09/condo-hoa-fees.html), and fees can rise up to 20% annually without a homeowner vote under current state law.

New construction in undeveloped areas of California also often comes with [Mello-Roos](https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-10/2023_1.pdf) special tax assessments, which fund infrastructure like roads, schools, and utilities in newly developed areas and are layered on top of regular property taxes — typically adding another monthly fee to new-build homes for years.

California’s home insurance market also compounds the problem. Some state insurers have [stopped providing coverage in many of the wildfire-prone areas](https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CA%20lot%20of%20other%20insurers%20have%20stopped%20selling%2C%E2%80%9D%20said%20Amy%20Bach%2C%20executive%20director%20of%20United%20Policyholders%2C%20a%20consumer%20group.%20%E2%80%9CIf%20you%20talk%20to%20an%20agent%20or%20broker%20today%2C%20they%E2%80%99re%20going%20to%20tell%20you%20it%20can%20be%20pretty%20hard%20to%20find%20insurance%E2%80%9D%20outside%20of%20the%20FAIR%20plan%2C%20Bach%20said.%C2%A0) where new homes are being built which has statewide ramifications. California’s state-run insurer of last resort, known as the FAIR Plan, is [likely to be overburdened](https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=As%20the%20risk%20of%20catastrophic%20wildfire%20ramps%20up%20across%20California%2C%20that%20risk%20falls%20disproportionately%20on%20the%20FAIR%20Plan.) to the extent that more insurers drop coverage across the state.

While home insurance challenges are not unique to Prop. 37, they remain acute in the wildland-urban interface — where [almost 45% of the houses built in California have been located](https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/01/ca-wui-housing-policy/#:~:text=Between%201990%20and,in%20the%20state.) over the last 30 years. Though these areas tend to have [less expensive real estate](https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/01/ca-wui-housing-policy/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CPeople%20are%20looking%20to%20the%20\(wildland%2Durban%20interface\)%20as%20one%20of%20the%20only%20places%20that%20has%20capacity%20for%20housing%2C%E2%80%9D%20she%20said.%20Though%20the%20wildland%2Durban%20interface%20includes%20toney%20enclaves%20of%20wealth%20like%20Pacific%20Palisades%2C%20it%20also%20features%20some%20of%20the%20more%20affordable%20real%20estate%20left%20in%20the%20state.), they are also particularly susceptible to wildfires. That exposure could mean higher premiums, more difficulty securing a loan, or dependence on the FAIR Plan, driving additional costs on top of the repayments of Prop. 37.

Altogether, these compounding factors could undercut the affordability gains the measure is purported to provide for Californians. As a result, the benefits of Prop. 37 may skew toward eligible families with greater financial resources who were already better positioned to cover the costs of homeownership.

## **Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?**

There have been [some official supporters](https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_37,_Second_Mortgage_Homebuyer_Program_and_Revenue_Bond_Initiative_\(2026\)#google_vignette:~:text=Who%20supports%20and%20opposes%20the%20initiative%3F) of the initiative, but no official opponents as of mid-summer 2026. Former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Robert Hertzberg is the primary sponsor and a supporter of this proposition. Hertzberg has stated the main goal of the measure is to [allow working families and their children to build wealth and remain in California](https://www.planningreport.com/2025/10/01/keeping-our-children-california-hertzberg-middle-class-homeownership-act).

Various carpentry-focused unions and realty organizations — like the California Association of Realtors and the Northern California Carpenters Regional Council — have also expressed support for the measure. Gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra has also expressed support for this measure.
